uncited: Unlike standard 3DGS which relies on opacity thresholds and stops densifying mid-training, these methods actively eliminate redundant primitives throughout the optimization process [12710-gaussian-volume-mask.md].

They are distinguished from sibling methods like [Exponentially Ascending Gradient Threshold](9684-exponentially-ascending-gradient-threshold.md) by using explicit geometric or volume-based criteria rather than gradient magnitude alone [14019-visibility-based-pruning-for-3d-gaussian-splatting.md].
All methods in this family aim to reduce the Gaussian count $N$ by identifying and removing primitives that contribute negligibly to the final rendered image.
The core mechanism involves a selection criterion (binary mask, visibility count, or gradient threshold) applied to Gaussian attributes (scale, opacity, position).
**Selection Criterion:** A scalar value or binary flag is computed for each Gaussian $n$ to determine its "essentiality."
**Elimination:** Gaussians failing the criterion are removed from the scene representation.
**Integration:** Pruning is typically integrated into the training loop, either periodically (e.g., at densification intervals) or as a post-training refinement step.

**Loss Regularization:** Many methods introduce a regularization term to the loss function to encourage sparsity or guide the optimizer to shrink unneeded Gaussians before pruning [12710-gaussian-volume-mask.md][14019-visibility-based-pruning-for-3d-gaussian-splatting.md].
Choose this method when a strict, pre-defined number of Gaussians is required for deployment.

The proliferation of Gaussians in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) leads to high memory and storage costs, often including redundant primitives with negligible volume or transparency [12710-gaussian-volume-mask.md].
Standard 3DGS uses opacity-based pruning which may leave many redundant Gaussians [12710-gaussian-volume-mask.md].
